prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, which brought atomic time keeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: After reading all eight opening ballots I move my preferred configuration from B007 (IceCube, my opening first place) to B018, optical lattice clocks. It is the only shortlisted candidate that four colleagues put in their top three (Kroll and Lindroth rank it first, Olsson third, Johansson fourth, and I had it second), and the support comes from members with different tastes, which is more informative than any one first place. On the merits it is the kind of result I trust: a new measurement technique (Lamb-Dicke trapping at the magic wavelength) that delivered a new capability, fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, and that has been reproduced and compared across many independent laboratories (Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and others). The credit is unusually clean for a modern experiment. Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and demonstrated the first strontium clock. Ye's group drove accuracy and stability to the record level and the many-body clock. Two names, no collaboration-scale credit problem, and five of five members who ranked it proposed exactly this pair. The physics will last, with direct uses in relativistic geodesy, tests of constants and dark-matter searches, and a redefinition of the second under discussion.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with earlier precision-measurement prizes. The 2005 prize covered the optical frequency comb (Hall and Haensch, with whom Ye worked), and 2012 covered control of single quantum systems for ion clocks (Wineland). A committee could read lattice clocks as a second-generation refinement of already recognised ideas rather than a distinct discovery. There is also a timing argument that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the application is still ahead of the prize. Other contributors, such as Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto and the Yb and Hg efforts, are not credited. Separately, I still think B007 is the most compelling discovery in my own field. I downgrade it only because a three-name credit out of a collaboration of several hundred, with Yoshida's role unclear to me, is hard to defend, and because source identification beyond TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 is still thin.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B018 first as precision measurement used as a discovery tool: a magic-wavelength lattice with the Doppler and recoil shifts removed, independent confirmation by many groups, and a clean two-name credit with Katori and Ye.
responses.response: I agree and it changes my own ordering. You and I weigh instrument-driven results in a similar way, and your point that many species and laboratories reproduce the performance answers the question I always ask, namely independent confirmation. I disagree mildly with your suggestion that we might wait for the SI second redefinition. A prize that waits for a metrology committee ties our decision to someone else's calendar, and the scientific case is already complete. On the attribution, I would like you or Lindroth to say whether Ye's share is the accuracy and many-body work or also the comb-based infrastructure, because only the first is new relative to 2005.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B018 first as precision atomic physics at its best, with Katori's lattice concept and Ye's accuracy records, repeated in many laboratories, and she admits the overlap with the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-trap prizes could look incremental to some.
responses.response: You are the expert on atomic structure here, so I accept your view that the magic-wavelength condition is a new physical idea and not a refinement of ion-trap control. I do not want to wave away the overlap worry myself. The 2012 prize was about individual trapped ions with a very small signal. The lattice clock gets its stability from interrogating thousands of neutral atoms at once, which is a different route to the performance, and I think we should say that explicitly in the citation. You also note that you cannot verify the current record uncertainties. Neither can I from these files, so we should ask the expert reviewers to confirm the 1e-18 claims and the inter-laboratory comparisons before the final ballot.

responses.point: Johansson puts circuit QED first, with strong light-matter coupling on a chip and the architecture of superconducting processors, and sees B018 only fourth, as a refinement of precision-measurement prizes already given. He also declares his own proximity to the circuit QED field.
responses.response: I respect the declaration, and I rank B008 fifth myself. I disagree on the main point. Your view of the clock as a refinement understates what changed: the lattice clock is a different way of building a clock, and it moved performance by orders of magnitude, whereas cQED mostly reuses cavity QED ideas in a new medium. I share your concern about timing but weigh it the other way. Only a year after the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, I think a second circuit prize looks premature, and the unresolved fourth name (Girvin versus Blais) would cost us time in the final round. I would keep B008 as a serious alternative for a later year.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first: a theory-predicted flat band followed by a surprising experimental phase diagram, reproduced widely, with the pairing mechanism still debated, and he would accept MacDonald plus Jarillo-Herrero if we want two names.
responses.response: I put B044 seventh, partly because condensed matter is outside my expertise, so I take your account of the band structure and the reproduction by many groups seriously. Our disagreement is about timing. Seven members ranked it, so the breadth of support is real, but you and Johansson both note that the pairing mechanism is unresolved and that credit within the Jarillo-Herrero group (Cao and Fatemi) is not captured by the three names. My test is whether the physics will last, and for a field that is changing this fast I would rather wait. I would leave B044 as a strong alternative, and if the committee goes that way I would accept the two-name version of Jarillo-Herrero and MacDonald, with Bistritzer a possible third.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the gamma-ray burst afterglows (B038) first as a decisive observational result that settled a three-decade puzzle, calls recognition overdue, and flags the difficulty of a clean three-person split for BeppoSAX and the Caltech follow-up.
responses.response: I ranked B038 fourth and agree on the science. Afterglows are among the best-confirmed results in high-energy astrophysics, and Swift and Fermi have confirmed them repeatedly. I share your attribution worry and think it is the real obstacle: Costa and Frontera for the X-ray localisation are clear, but the optical and redshift step involves van Paradijs, Djorgovski and Kulkarni's group, and I cannot say from these files who is eligible or deceased. That uncertainty is why I do not put it ahead of a candidate whose credit is already settled. You and I both gave B007 some support, and I take your reading that the source identification is still at evidence level and that three names from a collaboration of hundreds is hard to defend.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as a distinct discovery or an extension of the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 trapped-ion prizes.
The exact current record uncertainties and the inter-laboratory comparisons, which I cannot verify from these files and which expert reviewers should confirm.
Whether a two-name credit (Katori and Ye) leaves out contributors to the lattice clock, such as Lemonde, Ludlow or Takamoto, in a way the committee finds unacceptable.
Whether I am discounting B007 too much, because my own field makes me more sensitive to collaboration-credit problems than to the strength of the discovery.
statement.conflict_note: I am a member of the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations and work in astroparticle physics at KTH. This touches B007 (IceCube neutrino astronomy, my own field, with likely contacts among its scientists) and B038 (gamma-ray burst afterglows, which relates to Fermi-LAT and my gamma-ray polarimetry plans), so I would consider recusing myself from the final decision if either is the leading candidate. No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B018, B044 or B008, which are outside my field.
